question: Innovation Fled to Math
content: Naval observes that the two biggest technological advancements of the last decade — AI and crypto — both happened in the math domain. He argues this is not coincidental: math is the last unregulated domain where builders can innovate without asking permission.
description: A policy maker asks why Silicon Valley's most transformative innovations in the past decade have been AI and crypto rather than physical products like new aircraft, drugs, or manufacturing processes. What would Naval identify as the root cause?
options: Physical innovation is simply harder than digital innovation
AI and crypto happened in the math domain — the last unregulated
Venture capital only funds software companies, not physical products
The best engineers all chose to work in AI and crypto by personal preference
answer: AI and crypto happened in the math domain — the last unregulated
explanation: Naval says: 'The two biggest advancements in tech in Silicon Valley in the last decade — AI and, before that, crypto — they're both in the math domain, because that's the last unregulated domain. When they start regulating frontier models and GPUs, that stops as well.'

question: The Asymmetric Slowdown
content: Blake Scholl identifies the fundamental incentive problem in regulation: approving a bad thing destroys your career, while blocking a good thing goes completely unnoticed. This creates a powerful bias toward inaction and delay in every regulatory agency.
description: An FDA reviewer must decide whether to approve a promising new drug. If the drug turns out to have hidden side effects, the reviewer will be hauled before Congress. If the reviewer delays approval while gathering more data, no one notices. How does Blake Scholl describe this dynamic?
options: The FDA has insufficient funding to hire enough qualified reviewers
It's totally asymmetric — if you approve a bad thing, your career
The pharmaceutical industry deliberately bribes FDA reviewers to delay drugs which is a critical factor to consider in this context
The FDA is staffed by incompetent bureaucrats who don't understand science
answer: It's totally asymmetric — if you approve a bad thing, your career
explanation: Blake says: 'If you approve a bad thing, your career is over. If you block a good thing, nobody notices. It creates an asymmetric slowdown.' The incentive structure punishes action and rewards delay — exactly the opposite of what innovation needs.

question: The Deep Problem Is Cultural
content: Max Hodak pushes back on the simple 'regulation bad' narrative, arguing that the real problem is deeper than regulatory reform. The risk aversion is baked into the beliefs of the American people — the voters who elect politicians and the public that punishes agencies for taking risks.
description: A tech founder blames 'corrupt politicians' for blocking every attempt to build faster. Max Hodak would argue this framing misses the deeper issue. What is the actual root cause of regulatory paralysis, according to Max?
options: Politicians are uniquely corrupt in the current administration which is a critical factor to consider in this context
The risk aversion reflects the beliefs of the voters who elect those
Regulatory agencies are underfunded by a deliberate sabotage campaign
The media sensationalizes every failure, creating artificial public fear
answer: The risk aversion reflects the beliefs of the voters who elect those
explanation: Max says: 'It's where the voters are. The reality is that this is reflective of the beliefs of the American people. There's a trade-off between the perception of risk taken in human-subjects research, and the rate at which we get new medicines.' You can't fix regulation without addressing what voters want.

question: China's CFDA Is Beating the FDA
content: Max Hodak reveals that China's drug and medical device regulator (CFDA) is thinking for itself and approving technologies faster than the US. There is already an approved, getting-paid implantable brain-computer interface in China — something the US hasn't achieved yet.
description: You're developing a brain-computer interface medical device. The US regulatory pathway is projected to take seven years and $100 million. Your Chinese competitor has already received CFDA approval. What does this suggest about the competitive landscape?
options: Chinese regulators have lower safety standards and their approvals don't matter
The CFDA is thinking for itself and costs to bring products to market are
The US will never approve BCI devices for ethical reasons
Your competitor likely bribed the CFDA to get fast-track approval which is a critical factor to consider in this context
answer: The CFDA is thinking for itself and costs to bring products to market are
explanation: Max says: 'There actually is one approved, getting-paid implantable BCI today, which is in China. The CFDA is thinking for itself. The costs to bring a drug or device to market are just much lower. You can try things in humans and try things on market.'

question: Europe's Notified Body System
content: Max Hodak describes a different approach to regulatory review used in Europe: notified bodies. These are private businesses blessed by their host governments to certify products like trains, planes, and medical devices. They can hire more people, grow, and compete — unlike government agencies with fixed budgets.
description: A policy advisor proposes reforming the FDA by simply hiring more reviewers. Max Hodak suggests looking at Europe's system instead. How does Europe's regulatory model differ from the US approach?
options: Europe has no regulatory oversight for medical devices at all
Europe uses private notified bodies that compete, creating better
Europe uses military hospitals to test all new medical devices
Europe outsources all medical device regulation to the WHO
answer: Europe uses private notified bodies that compete, creating better
explanation: Max says Europe's notified bodies are 'basically private businesses blessed by their host governments to certify things. The notified-body system creates slightly better incentives at the review layer because they can hire people, they can grow, there's competition.'

question: Healthcare Is a Communist Society
content: Naval uses a powerful restaurant analogy to explain why healthcare doesn't improve like other industries. Imagine eating at restaurants and sending the bill to your insurer at month-end — every good restaurant would have lines, and bad restaurants would thrive because nobody pays directly.
description: Your friend argues that healthcare would work fine if we just had a single-payer system like other countries. Using Naval's restaurant analogy, what fundamental problem does third-party payment create in any industry?
options: Single-payer systems always have better outcomes than private insurance
Without direct payment, there's no price signal — no feedback loop for
Restaurant and healthcare economics are completely incomparable which is a critical factor to consider in this context
Single-payer works for restaurants in countries with nationalized hospitality
answer: Without direct payment, there's no price signal — no feedback loop for
explanation: Naval's restaurant analogy: if you ate at restaurants and sent all receipts to the government, 'There'd be a line outside every good restaurant. Every bad restaurant would be available. The waits would be terrible. The product wouldn't improve.' The feedback loop of direct payment drives improvement.

question: The LASIK Proof
content: Naval points to elective medical procedures as proof that private markets drive innovation in healthcare. LASIK, dental veneers, braces, and plastic surgery have all improved significantly because patients pay out of pocket and vote with their money.
description: A policy maker claims that 'healthcare is fundamentally different and market forces cannot improve it.' What counter-evidence would Naval cite to demonstrate that private payment does drive medical innovation?
options: No medical field has ever improved through market forces
LASIK, dental surgery, and plastic surgery have all advanced because they
European single-payer systems have the best cosmetic surgery in the world
Private payment leads to worse outcomes because patients can't evaluate quality
answer: LASIK, dental surgery, and plastic surgery have all advanced because they
explanation: Naval says: 'Look at optometry with LASIK. Look at dental with veneers and braces and dental surgery. Look at plastic surgery. Those fields do seem to be advancing because they're private payers — people voting with their money.'

question: The 20% Deductible Thought Experiment
content: Naval proposes a provocative thought experiment: make the first 20% of every person's annual income their healthcare deductible. For a broke person it's zero; for a wealthy person it's millions. The rest is covered by insurance and government. This would create a private market where people spend their own money on healthcare.
description: During a healthcare policy discussion, someone asks how to create market dynamics in medicine without abandoning universal coverage. What is Naval's 20% deductible thought experiment designed to achieve?
options: Eliminate all health insurance and make everyone pay out of pocket
Create a private market where people spend their own first dollars on
Shift all healthcare costs to employers to create corporate accountability
Replace all doctors with AI to reduce the cost of medical procedures
answer: Create a private market where people spend their own first dollars on
explanation: Naval proposes: 'The first 20% of your annual income was your healthcare deductible. If you're broke and homeless, it's zero. If you're rich, it's millions.' This creates a private market for the first 20% of spending, where people shop around and drive quality competition.

question: The Fixed Healthcare Bucket
content: Max Hodak identifies a structural difference between healthcare and every other technology industry. When phones got cheaper and better, people bought more phones — total spending went up, and everyone was happy. In healthcare, the total spending is roughly fixed, determined by tax receipts, not value delivered.
description: Your healthcare startup creates a device that reduces heart surgery costs by 90%. In a normal industry, this would drive massive adoption. According to Max Hodak, what happens instead because healthcare has a 'fixed bucket' of money?
options: Hospitals immediately adopt the device and pass savings to patients
The fixed reimbursement system means total healthcare spending doesn't
Insurance companies pay a bonus to startups that reduce costs
The government subsidizes the device to encourage rapid adoption
answer: The fixed reimbursement system means total healthcare spending doesn't
explanation: Max explains: 'The bucket of money we use to buy healthcare is basically fixed. It is not increasing as there's more stuff producing better healthcare outcomes, the way we see in technological growth industries. The rate of spending grows at roughly the rate of growth of tax receipts.'
